rows.stage: Trust — the proof a skeptic needs
rows.visitor: A skeptical evaluator who likes the pitch but has been burned by hype. They want sourced numbers, an honest ledger, a clear comparison, and a real license before they invest more time.
rows.job: See that the claims are backed (a benchmark authority, an honesty ledger where every claim carries a status tag), understand how fak differs from what they already run, and confirm it is real open source.

affordances.need: a benchmark-authority doc every headline figure traces to — the number is sourced, not asserted

the honesty ledger (CLAIMS.md) backs the core product claim with a status tag, so a claim can be trusted instead of discounted (CLAIMS.md tags the product claim SHIPPED with a witness page; the ledger is a single ## Claims section of tagged claim links since the #9232 managed index)
the front page links the honesty ledger — the skeptic can reach the tagged claims in one hop
a positioning/comparison surface answering 'how is this different from the thing I already use'

honest boundary statements on the front page naming what fak is NOT — llama.cpp is never a silent fallback, per-result parity/quality fences beside every number — the fastest trust-builder for a skeptic (the #9751 latest-hardware front page)
a social-proof / adoption surface (witnessed usage, directory presence) for 'other people use this'
a real OSS license file, so the visitor confirms they can actually use it
a catalogue of supported models/engines/harnesses — breadth-of-support proof

gaps: Social proof today is witnessed-usage + directory submissions; named third-party testimonials are honest-scope-fenced until they exist

rows.visitor: A convinced visitor who wants the binary now. The friction between 'interested' and 'have it running' is where they leak if the path is unclear or broken.
rows.job: Get fak with one command that resolves — a go install one-liner (module at the repo root) or a prebuilt archive — with a fuller install doc for the other platforms.

affordances.need: the go install ...@latest one-liner on the front page (the module is at the repo root, so it resolves)
the EXACT installable module path, so `go install ...@latest` resolves directly — a stale path fails this
a fuller install doc (prebuilt archives, containers, per-platform notes) for the visitor who cannot go install
a no-toolchain path to the binary (a curl|sh installer or a release-artifacts CI job) for the visitor who will not build from source

gaps: No Homebrew/winget/scoop package yet — the lowest-effort install is curl|sh, a release archive, or go install

rows.visitor: A visitor with the binary who wants a first success in under a minute — a command that runs with no key/model/GPU and prints an observable result they can recognize as 'it worked'.
rows.job: Run one offline command and see a labelled result (a cost/quality delta, a DENY verdict), backed by a quickstart from clone and a demo doc that shows what else to run.

affordances.need: a copy-pasteable no-key/no-model/no-GPU first command in a fenced block
an observable success signal shown inline with the first command (an expected result marker), so the visitor can tell it WORKED
the first command's verb actually resolves against the binary's dispatch (documented in the CLI reference) — a doc that names a dead verb is an ambush
a quickstart/tutorial that carries the visitor from clone to a running kernel
a demo doc that shows the visitor what else to run after the first win

gaps: The first win is a deterministic offline lens (routebench/preflight); a hosted one-click demo would remove the install step entirely for the lowest-effort visitor
